content.text:
Yes. In the U.S., there are several **teaching fields where schools consistently report not having enough qualified people**, especially at the K–12 level. The shortages are not evenly spread across all subjects or locations—they’re usually concentrated in certain specialties and in rural, high-poverty, or hard-to-staff districts.

**Common shortage teaching fields include:**

1. **Special education**  
   This is probably the most persistent shortage area. A 2024–25 analysis found that **45 states** reported special education teacher shortages. ([learningpolicyinstitute.org](https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/teacher-shortages-subjects-across-states-factsheet?utm_source=openai))

2. **Math**  
   Secondary math teachers are often hard to hire, partly because people with strong math backgrounds have many non-teaching career options. Math was reported as a shortage area in **40 states** for 2024–25. ([learningpolicyinstitute.org](https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/teacher-shortages-subjects-across-states-factsheet?utm_source=openai))

3. **Science**, especially **physics and chemistry**  
   Science was reported as a shortage area in **41 states**. The American Association for Employment in Education also notes continuing “considerable shortage” in special education, physics, chemistry, and math. ([learningpolicyinstitute.org](https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/teacher-shortages-subjects-across-states-factsheet?utm_source=openai))

4. **Bilingual education / ESL / English learner instruction**  
   Many districts struggle to find teachers qualified to teach multilingual learners. NCES reported that among high schools with vacancies in ESL or bilingual education, **69%** had difficulty filling those positions with fully certified teachers for the 2024–25 school year. ([nces.ed.gov](https://nces.ed.gov/learn/press-release/most-u-s-public-elementary-and-secondary-schools-faced-hiring-challenges-start-2024-25-academic-year?utm_source=openai))

5. **World languages**  
   Foreign/world language teachers are also commonly listed as shortage areas; the Learning Policy Institute found world languages reported by **35 states** in 2024–25. ([learningpolicyinstitute.org](https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/media/4754/download?file=Teacher_Shortages_by_Subject_FACTSHEET.pdf&inline=&utm_source=openai))

6. **Career and technical education — CTE**  
   Fields like agriculture, skilled trades, business/technology, health occupations, and computer science can be hard to staff because qualified people may earn more in industry. CTE was reported as a shortage area by **33 states** in 2024–25. ([learningpolicyinstitute.org](https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/media/4754/download?file=Teacher_Shortages_by_Subject_FACTSHEET.pdf&inline=&utm_source=openai))

7. **Computer science / instructional technology**  
   This varies by state, but it is increasingly listed as a shortage area; for example, Colorado’s 2025–26 shortage list includes computer science/instructional technology. ([ed.cde.state.co.us](https://ed.cde.state.co.us/educatortalent/researchandimpact/colorados-educator-shortage-survey-results?utm_source=openai))

Fields that are **less likely** to have shortages, depending on location, include elementary education, social studies/history, English language arts, art, and physical education—though even those can be short in specific districts. The key point is that “teacher shortage” usually means **shortages in specific fields and locations**, not that every teaching job is easy to get.
